History:
• 45-year-old male presents with 5-day history of “cough and cold.”  
• Onset: began over the weekend (~5 days ago); gradual.  
• Symptoms: dry, hacking cough; runny nose; generalized myalgias; chills; occasional headache.  
• Denies sputum production, hemoptysis, shortness of breath, wheeze, or chest tightness.  
• No palpable neck glands reported. No prior similar severe episodes stated.  
• Self-care: paracetamol; no ibuprofen. Has not used OTC cold combinations yet.

Past Medical History:
• Type 2 diabetes mellitus × 5–6 years.  
• Mild hypertension.  
• Allergies: Not recorded.  
• Medications:  
  – Metformin – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  – Lisinopril – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  – Paracetamol (acetaminophen) as needed – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Home blood-pressure this morning “within normal range.” Self-monitors blood glucose—reports normal readings.

Physical Examination:
• General: Appears well on video, conversational, no respiratory distress.  
• HEENT: Mild pharyngeal erythema; no tonsillar hypertrophy or exudate; no visible cervical lymphadenopathy.  
• Respiratory: No wheeze or audible rattles reported; lungs not auscultated (virtual visit).  
• Cardiovascular, Abdomen, Extremities, Neuro, Skin: Not recorded.  
• Vitals: Not recorded (patient only reports normal BP).

Impression:
Most consistent with an uncomplicated viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold).  
Alternate considerations (consistent with DDx):  
1. Influenza-like illness – systemic aches/chills could reflect early influenza.  
2. ACE-inhibitor (lisinopril)–related cough – less likely given concurrent rhinorrhea and systemic symptoms.

Management Plan:
• Symptomatic therapy: advised OTC Day Nurse/Night Nurse preparations; safe with metformin and lisinopril.  
• Continue paracetamol as needed for aches/fever.  
• No antibiotics or prescriptions required at this time.  
• Red-flag advice: seek care if new shortness of breath, wheeze, chest pain, hemoptysis, or if symptoms persist >3 weeks or significantly worsen.  
• Routine diabetes and BP medications to continue unchanged.  
• No immediate investigations or imaging indicated.

Patient Summary:
Mr. John Jones, a 45-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and mild hypertension, presents with a 5-day dry cough, rhinorrhea, and mild systemic symptoms consistent with a viral URTI. Examination shows only mild pharyngeal erythema. He is managed conservatively with OTC symptomatic relief and safety-net advice.

Key Takeaways:
• Start Day Nurse/Night Nurse for symptomatic relief; may continue paracetamol.  
• Return for assessment if breathing becomes difficult, symptoms last >3 weeks, or overall condition deteriorates.

Next Steps:
• None immediately. Monitor symptoms at home.  
• Follow up with primary care if red-flag symptoms develop or no improvement by 3 weeks.

• Transcript–DDx conflicts: none noted.  
• Transcript quality: clear audio; limited physical exam inherent to virtual visit.
